messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Product Manager
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun Patel was 58 when he came to treatment, a married South Asian American man who worked as a product manager for a large technology company. He described the event that divided his life into “before and after” as a period of torture during a trip abroad several years earlier. He had been detained without warning by men in uniform, taken to a cramped holding area, and questioned in a language he only partly understood. What remained most vivid to him was not a coherent sequence but a series of sharply felt moments: the noise of several voices speaking over one another in rapid, incomprehensible bursts; the shrill rise and fall of sirens outside; the sudden spinning sensation in his body when he was exhausted, dehydrated, and terrified; and the sight of uniforms and weapons entering his field of vision before anyone spoke to him directly. He remembered trying to make sense of what was being said, straining for a familiar word and finding none, while believing that whatever happened next would be decided by men he could not understand and could not stop.

In the months after he returned home, Arjun found that ordinary life no longer felt ordinary. In meetings at work, when side conversations broke out among colleagues in languages he did not know, his attention snagged immediately. He was no longer simply hearing office chatter; his body tightened as if he were back in that holding area, trying to decode sounds that seemed to carry danger. If an ambulance passed the building and sirens cut through the conference room windows, he lost the thread of what anyone was saying. He would sit very still, waiting for the sound to fade, embarrassed by how quickly his heart raced and how completely the rest of the room disappeared for a few seconds. When he felt dizzy or lightheaded—after standing up too fast, skipping lunch during a product launch, or standing in a hot crowded elevator—he became intensely alert. Rather than dismissing it, he checked himself repeatedly for signs that something was wrong, scanning for injury, weakness, or some bodily signal that he was not actually safe.

At home, his wife noticed that he no longer moved through the house with ease. If she touched his shoulder unexpectedly while he was washing dishes or reading on the couch, he jolted violently before he could recognize her. He hated the look of hurt and surprise on her face and would apologize, but he also felt he could not control it. Even in familiar places he could not settle. He said that relaxing felt irresponsible, as though lowering his guard would invite something terrible. At night he woke abruptly and checked the locks, the hallway, the windows, orienting himself to where he was before lying back down. He knew he was in his own home, knew on one level that he was safe, but that knowledge did not bring the bodily sense of safety other people seemed to take for granted.

Over time he organized his life around preventing strain. He began avoiding anything he thought might be stressful: difficult client calls, crowded commuting days, family events likely to be noisy or chaotic. At work he delegated presentations he once handled easily and sometimes left the office by a back route if police officers were visible near the entrance or if a security demonstration involved uniformed personnel. He did not tell colleagues why; he simply said he had another meeting. The cost accumulated quietly. His team experienced him as more withdrawn and less available under pressure, and at home his world narrowed. His wife wanted to visit friends, go into the city, make plans for the future, and Arjun often found reasons to stay in.

What weighed on him most was not only fear but the conclusions he had drawn about himself and other people. He had come to believe that people could not be trusted, especially anyone carrying authority, and he extended that suspicion broadly, even when he disliked doing so. Alongside that was a quieter, more corrosive conviction that there was something about him that had made the torture happen—that he had been the kind of person to whom such things could be done. When he spoke about the future, he did so flatly. Nothing good can happen to me anymore, he said, not dramatically but as if stating a fact he had tested many times.

He finally sought help after an incident at work in which a coworker came up behind him during a tense launch week and put a hand on his arm to get his attention just as sirens sounded outside. Arjun spun around in alarm, knocking his chair sideways, and the silence that followed in the room stayed with him for days. He was shaken less by the embarrassment than by the recognition that his life had become organized around vigilance, retreat, and the expectation of harm. When he came in, what frightened him most was the idea that this was permanent—that he would remain a man who could not trust, could not rest, and could not imagine a future larger than staying safe. What he hoped for, cautiously, was not to forget what happened but to be able to live in his office, his home, and his own body without waiting for danger to return.
